s: Traditional message broker supporting flexible routing topologies, priority queues, and per-message acknowledgments.
w: Producers publish to exchanges (direct, topic, fanout, headers) which route to queues based on binding keys. Consumers pull or get pushed; manual ack ensures at-least-once delivery. TTL, dead-letter exchanges, and priority queues provide built-in job management. Quorum queues (Raft-based) give replication for durability. Lightweight compared to Kafka for traditional messaging.
use: Task distribution with complex routing: per-type queues, priority jobs
Legacy enterprise integration replacing or wrapping older MQ systems
Small-to-medium throughput systems needing flexible routing without Kafka's weight
avoid: High-throughput log streaming (Kafka's append-only log is far more efficient)
Long-term message replay (RabbitMQ deletes on ack; Kafka retains)
Event sourcing stores (no durable log semantics)

size.messages_per_sec: ~20k-50k per node depending on persistence settings

pat.d: Multiple workers dequeue from one queue distributing load automatically.

pits: Unacked messages pile up during consumer crashes - set prefetch and per-consumer limits
Memory alarms triggering flow control - monitor queue depths and disk alarms proactively
tips: vs Kafka: RabbitMQ = smart routing + per-message ack, Kafka = high-throughput ordered log
Exchange routing topology is RabbitMQ's strength - model it explicitly in design interviews
